about: The advisor findings we accept on purpose (ARCHITECTURE §8.2 rule 4, §11.6). npm run sql:advisors compares get_advisors output (security and performance) with this file: a finding that matches no entry fails, and a required entry with no finding fails. Every entry says why it is accepted. Edit it in the same pull request as the migration that causes the finding.

live.note: Before SQL-1 the project held only CNT-0's private.key_escrow, and both advisors reported nothing. A restrictive deny-all policy counts as a policy for lint 0008.

rpc.why: Every RPC is a SECURITY DEFINER function in public that anon is meant to call; that is the whole API (§8.2 rule 2). Lint 0028 flags each one for anon and lint 0029 for authenticated, which keeps EXECUTE because migrations never take a grant away (decisions memo §14.4). Each RPC validates its input, caps payloads and rate-limits itself, so both findings are expected for exactly these names. The list mirrors private.rpc_allowlist: npm run sql:bundle checks that the two agree, and the ticket that adds an RPC adds its name to both. SQL-1 adds none.

accepted.why: The hourly job prunes counters older than 2 days through this index. Until pg_cron runs it (SQL-8) and the table grows past a few pages, no plan uses it, so INFO 0005 reports it as unused.
The hourly job prunes write keys older than 48 hours through this index; unused until the job runs over a table large enough to scan by index.
delete_player (SQL-2) removes a player's write keys by player id with this index, so the deletion stays an index lookup (AC-DAT-02). Nothing uses it before SQL-2.

§8.3 indexes the error log by time for the owner's triage through MCP: an internal reply shows its reference, and the owner reads the errors logged around it. Nothing reads the log before the first RPC that can fail (SQL-2), so INFO 0005 reports the index as unused.
